title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
summary: We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.

AI.tldr: Shows that agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, for classes with VC dimension d and diameter K, needs sample complexity of order K^(1/3) d^(2/3) / eps up to log factors, improving the earlier K/eps upper bound and matching it on some classes.
AI.motivation: Prior work gave an upper bound of K/eps for deterministic-label agnostic learning but left a large gap to the lower bounds, so the true sample complexity of this intermediate setting between realizable and fully agnostic learning was unclear.
AI.method: The upper bounds come from memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure, and the authors construct classes showing the bound is tight up to logarithmic factors; they also study the online analogue.
AI.result: Every class with VC dimension d and finite diameter K is learnable with sample complexity of order K^(1/3) d^(2/3) / eps up to logarithmic factors, and the bound is tight for some constructed classes; the minimax online regret is also partly controlled by the diameter.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic labels provably reduce the cost of agnostic learning relative to the classical O(d/eps^2) rate, and the diameter of the class governs both the sample complexity and the online regret in this setting.

title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
summary: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.

AI.tldr: Proposes MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction for causal mediation analysis and produces confidence intervals with near-nominal coverage.
AI.motivation: Confidence intervals for causal mediation estimates must account for uncertainty from fitting and combining several nuisance functions, and existing approaches such as the bootstrap are computationally expensive.
AI.method: A tabular foundation model supplies conditional mean and propensity score estimates that are combined through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator; a separate head learns quantiles of the standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects, followed by supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization and independent calibration.
AI.result: The coverage bounds are established under standard assumptions; in experiments MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators and runs 59.1 times faster than the bootstrap in matched comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Amortized inference with a pretrained tabular foundation model offers a faster route to valid uncertainty quantification for causal mediation analysis than resampling-based methods.

title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
comment: International Journal of Forecasting (Work in progress paper)
summary: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.

AI.tldr: Introduces Continuous Horizon (CH) forecasting, which treats the forecast as a continuous operator with the horizon as a query variable, and shows it is competitive in RMSE on 16 M-series datasets while enabling parallel inference and interpolation across horizons.
AI.motivation: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete strategies (recursive, direct, multi-step) that treat outputs as fixed vectors or generate them recurrently, which limits flexibility across horizons.
AI.method: The CH strategy generalizes recursive, direct and multi-step strategies by redefining the forecast as a continuous operator and the horizon as a query variable, supported by a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition.
AI.result: On a simulation study and 16 large-scale M-series datasets, CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, the decomposition shows variance improvements over discrete strategies, and the method supports parallel inference, targeted horizon querying and interpolation and extrapolation to unseen horizons.
AI.conclusion: Treating the forecast horizon as a continuous query variable gives a theoretically grounded alternative to discrete multi-horizon strategies with competitive accuracy and extra flexibility.

title: Time Series Change Point Detection with Gaussian Processes
summary: This paper proposes a novel general Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series. A change is defined as an alteration of the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process prior. We formulate the problem in the context of statistical hypothesis testing and demonstrate its performance over both offline and online multiple change points detection. The approach provides theoretical guaranties of its performance. An important advantage of the developed framework is that it does not need a detailed specification of the time series function before and after a change. The hyperparameter values are learned from the data. Comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework is provided both on synthetic and real data and its efficiency is demonstrated.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Gaussian process framework for change point detection in time series, defining a change as a shift in the GP prior hyperparameters, and tests it for offline and online detection of multiple change points.
AI.motivation: Change point detection usually requires a detailed specification of the time series function before and after each change, which is often unavailable.
AI.method: Changes are cast as alterations of the hyperparameters of a Gaussian process prior, the problem is formulated as statistical hypothesis testing, and hyperparameters are learned from the data without specifying the functional form of the series.
AI.result: The approach is evaluated on synthetic and real data for both offline and online multiple change point detection, and the authors report that its efficiency is demonstrated; the abstract states theoretical performance guarantees.
AI.conclusion: A general GP hyperparameter view of change points yields a flexible detection framework that does not need explicit models of the pre- and post-change behaviour.

title: VC-Dimension and Generalization in Geometric Machine Learning with Applications to Active Learning
summary: We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.

AI.tldr: Computes the VC dimension of metric ball classifiers in Riemannian model spaces (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and gives bounds for normed spaces, l^p norms, flat tori and general Riemannian manifolds, then derives covering-based generalization bounds for low-dimensional data.
AI.motivation: The VC dimension of metric balls in general geometric and normed settings was not well characterized, and generalization guarantees are needed when the VC dimension is large or infinite.
AI.method: The authors compute exact VC dimensions for the model spaces and derive upper and lower bounds for other settings, then prove generalization bounds under extra distributional assumptions using covering arguments applied to data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
AI.result: The VC dimension is infinite for general normed spaces, grows at least linearly with dimension for l^p norms and faster than Euclidean for p=1, and can be arbitrarily large for general Riemannian manifolds after a conformal change; covering-based bounds hold even when the VC dimension is large or infinite.
AI.conclusion: Geometry strongly controls the complexity of metric ball classifiers, and covering arguments give usable generalization guarantees where VC analysis fails, with an application to coverage-based active learning.

title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
summary: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.

AI.tldr: Develops differentially private score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy, giving finite-sample error bounds, asymptotically valid confidence intervals and bootstrap confidence sets for ranks, applied to ranking large language models for creative writing.
AI.motivation: Ranking large language models from human pairwise comparisons must protect the privacy of individual preference records, and existing inference procedures do not provide valid private uncertainty quantification for scores and ranks.
AI.method: The authors use an objective-perturbed estimator analysed with a leave-one-out argument, add a plug-in ridge-bias correction together with Gaussian-Laplace calibration to handle regularization bias and privacy noise, and establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference.
AI.result: Finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise errors are established, asymptotic confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise differences are valid, bootstrap confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-K membership are asymptotically valid, and no extra privacy budget is needed when the comparison probability is public; simulations evaluate finite-sample performance.
AI.conclusion: Private inference for Bradley-Terry scores and ranks is feasible with valid intervals and rank sets, so privacy-preserving rankings of language models can carry statistically sound uncertainty.

title: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
summary:
Simulation optimization typically returns a single estimated optimal point. When decisions also depend on criteria evaluated independently of simulation, such as resource cost, the decision maker instead needs the set of designs whose expected performance lies within a tolerance of the optimum, often choosing the tolerance only after seeing the tradeoffs. We study how to identify these near-optimal regions on a continuous design space, simultaneously for all tolerances up to a prescribed maximum $T$, with region estimation error at most $\eta$. We show that region identification is not a by-product of optimization. Specifically, when $\alpha>
u$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $\Omega igl(\eta^{-(2+d/
u)}\min\{1,KT^{d/\alpha}\} igr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $
u$ the smoothness, and $(K,\alpha)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. We propose SASORI, which returns an estimated optimal point and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching this lower bound up to logarithmic factors. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

AI.tldr: Introduces SASORI, which identifies near-optimal regions for all tolerances up to a maximum T from the same simulation evaluations and returns an estimated optimal point, matching a minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: Simulation optimization returns a single optimal point, but decisions that depend on external criteria such as cost need the whole set of designs within a tolerance of the optimum, with the tolerance chosen after seeing trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors prove a minimax lower bound on the number of evaluations needed for region identification, depending on dimension, smoothness and covering parameters (K, alpha), and design SASORI, an adaptive sampling procedure that estimates the optimum and the regions for all tolerances jointly.
AI.result: The lower bound shows region identification is not a by-product of optimization when alpha is greater than nu; SASORI matches this bound up to logarithmic factors, achieves the optimal trade-off between region error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal optimizer at zero tolerance; numerical experiments illustrate its effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Near-optimal regions can be identified at the minimax rate simultaneously for all tolerances, so practitioners get the full set of trade-off designs from a single run without extra simulation cost.

title: Outliers and the Hard-Margin Linear SVM in High-Dimension, Low-Sample-Size Settings
summary: We study how outliers affect the hard-margin linear support vector machine when the dimension grows while the sample sizes remain fixed. For one-sided contamination, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, and the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution. All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.

AI.tldr: Analyses the hard-margin linear SVM in high-dimension, low-sample-size settings under outlier contamination, deriving closed-form limiting dual solutions and explicit thresholds for support loss, margin shrinkage, intercept displacement and misclassification.
AI.motivation: The effect of outliers on the hard-margin linear SVM is not well understood when dimension grows while sample sizes stay fixed, which is the high-dimension low-sample-size regime.
AI.method: For one-sided contamination the centered Gram matrix is shown to converge to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, yielding a closed-form limiting dual; contamination in both classes is then treated via the class-balance constraint multiplier, and seven numerical experiments check the predictions.
AI.result: All outliers act through one effective distance, giving explicit thresholds for inlier support loss, margin shrinkage, intercept displacement and asymptotic misclassification; with two-class contamination at most one class can collapse or be misclassified, while symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant unchanged though the margin shrinks.
AI.conclusion: In this regime the impact of outliers reduces to a single effective distance and a class-allocation rule, so the asymptotic behaviour of the SVM under contamination can be characterized explicitly.

title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures with the IEEE Transactions template
summary: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.

AI.tldr: Proposes a moment problem based on transportation entropy for estimating the power spectral density of VARMA processes without fixing the moving-average component or restricting it to be scalar.
AI.motivation: Existing maximum-entropy spectral estimation methods for VARMA processes assume the MA component is fixed or scalar, which limits the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought.
AI.method: The spectral density is chosen to maximize an entropy-like index based on transportation entropy while matching certain moments of the process, with the MA component left free in the formulation.
AI.result: The abstract describes the proposed moment problem for learning the spectral density of VARMA processes with a general MA component; it does not report numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Transportation entropy extends moment-based spectral estimation to the general vector MA case, broadening the class of models that can be estimated.

title: Compositional random forest
summary: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.

AI.tldr: Builds random forests for compositional responses using log-likelihood split criteria on three representations of compositions: a tangent-normal distribution on the sphere, a logistic-normal distribution in log-ratio space, and the Dirichlet, which is discussed as a baseline.
AI.motivation: Compositional data are analysed on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates or as directional data, but the Dirichlet likelihood has covariance fixed by its mean and no closed-form MLE, which limits flexibility for tree splitting.
AI.method: The square-root transformation maps compositions to the unit sphere, where a new tangent-normal distribution sharing parameters with the Kent distribution gives a split gain from additive sufficient statistics with shape parameters maximized in closed form up to a tiny truncation constant; the log-ratio transformation gives a multivariate logistic-normal criterion with closed-form maximum log-likelihood.
AI.result: In simulations the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition, and the tangent-normal forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.
AI.conclusion: Choosing the split distribution to match the covariance structure of compositions improves random forest accuracy, and the tangent-normal criterion is a strong option when the covariance is non-trivial.

title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
comment: 27 pages main text, 57 pages supplementary material with 6 sections, 1 figure
summary: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.

AI.tldr: Gives an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of cross-validated estimates, showing that K-fold is first-order variance optimal, leave-one-out has the smallest variance among K-fold schemes, and leave-pair-out is best for AUC.
AI.motivation: Cross-validation variance is hard to analyse because each observation plays two roles, as a held-out evaluation point and as a training point, and existing guidance on choosing splitting schemes lacks a general theory.
AI.method: The authors express each observation's influence through its random weights in these two roles, prove an exact finite-sample variance identity covering averaged metrics such as MSE and pairwise metrics such as AUC, and decompose the variance into sampling and fold-splitting components.
AI.result: The sampling part depends only on training size, while the fold-splitting part arises when weights vary across draws; K-fold has equal weights and is first-order optimal, its first-order variance does not depend on K, and leave-one-out has the smallest variance among K-fold schemes; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not optimal; the estimate is asymptotically normal with the full variance.
AI.conclusion: The identity provides a general foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and a principled basis for choosing variance-optimal designs.

title: Geometry and Stochastic Analysis of Flow and Diffusion Models: A Survey
summary: Flow-based and diffusion-based models have become the principal means of learning and sampling high-dimensional probability distributions, from images and video to proteins, molecules and physical fields, and increasingly language. Each carries a simple law to the law of the data along a curve of probability measures, and behind the variety of their names lie three geometries, those of the state space on which the data live, of the space of probability measures through which the curve passes, and of the space of paths traced by the generating process. A single analytic idea runs through the subject. Every score identity used to train a diffusion model is an integration by parts, on the noise, on the data or on Wiener space, and Malliavin calculus extends this to nonlinear and infinite-dimensional diffusions. We develop these foundations with full definitions and follow them through normalising flows, flow matching and few-step maps, diffusion models and their convergence theory, conditioning, Schrödinger bridges and stochastic control, and their extension to manifolds, Lie groups, discrete and function spaces and jump processes. We close with statistical physics, renormalisation and, more speculatively, holography, in which the radial direction of anti-de Sitter space can play the role of flow time. A table of the main methods and a collection of open problems complete the survey.

AI.tldr: A survey of flow-based and diffusion-based generative models that organizes them through three geometries (state space, space of probability measures, space of paths), with Malliavin calculus and integration by parts as a unifying analytic tool.
AI.motivation: Flow and diffusion models are now the main tools for sampling high-dimensional distributions across many domains, but their theory is spread across separate subfields and lacks a unified geometric and stochastic treatment.
AI.method: The survey gives full definitions and develops normalising flows, flow matching and few-step maps, diffusion model convergence theory, conditioning, Schrödinger bridges and stochastic control, and extensions to manifolds, Lie groups, discrete spaces, function spaces and jump processes, with score identities cast as integration by parts.
AI.result: The survey provides a table of the main methods and a collection of open problems, and closes with links to statistical physics, renormalisation and, speculatively, holography, where the radial direction of anti-de Sitter space plays the role of flow time.
AI.conclusion: Viewing the field through three geometries and integration by parts gives a coherent foundation for flow and diffusion models and points to open problems across their extensions.

title: Generative Learning on Manifolds for Probabilistic Seismic Performance Assessment and Structural Identifiability
summary: Seismic performance assessment relies on computationally expensive nonlinear simulations, limiting uncertainty quantification and inference of structural properties from observed responses. We develop a manifold-based generative framework that learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and seismic-response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations. Combining Diffusion Maps, score-based Diffusion Modeling, and Geometric Harmonics, the framework enables both forward probabilistic prediction and inverse inference. Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the results reveal which structural properties are identifiable from seismic performance and how uncertainty in these properties influences response. In particular, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation characteristics more effectively than individual strength parameters. Inverse inference identifies distinct structural configurations that produce similar seismic performance, with representative solutions independently validated using nonlinear simulations. These findings demonstrate how generative learning can support uncertainty-aware seismic assessment while revealing structural non-identifiability and alternative mechanisms underlying observed performance

AI.tldr: Develops a manifold-based generative framework using Diffusion Maps, score-based diffusion modelling and Geometric Harmonics to learn the joint distribution of structural parameters and seismic response, enabling forward prediction and inverse inference for a nine-story steel frame.
AI.motivation: Seismic performance assessment depends on costly nonlinear simulations, which limits uncertainty quantification and inference of structural properties from observed responses.
AI.method: The framework learns the joint distribution of uncertain structural parameters and response trajectories from limited high-fidelity simulations, combining Diffusion Maps, score-based diffusion modelling and Geometric Harmonics for both forward and inverse problems.
AI.result: Applied to a nine-story steel moment-resisting frame, the learned representation captures post-capping degradation better than individual strength parameters, shows which properties are identifiable, and inverse inference finds distinct structural configurations with similar performance, with representative solutions validated by nonlinear simulation.
AI.conclusion: Generative learning on manifolds supports uncertainty-aware seismic assessment and reveals structural non-identifiability and alternative mechanisms behind observed performance.

title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Main Track, Poster
summary: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. Code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes ConceptTime, an interpretable time series classifier that uses the predictive surprise of a frozen forecaster to find segment boundaries, cluster segments into dynamical-regime concepts, and classify with a reliability-aware head, without annotations.
AI.motivation: Time series classifiers for risk-sensitive settings must be accurate, interpretable and able to abstain, but existing methods use fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, which sacrifices at least one of these properties because segment boundaries and patterns depend on each other.
AI.method: A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts the next observation at each timestep, and the mismatch with the realized signal, called predictive surprise, locates segment boundaries and characterizes segments, which are clustered into a concept vocabulary; a lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence and the distance to the nearest concept gives reliability.
AI.result: Across 17 public benchmarks ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline and retains near 98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels; it remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Grounding segments in expectation violations rather than appearance yields an accurate, interpretable and self-abstaining classifier that needs no annotation, language model or domain expert.

title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
summary: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

AI.tldr: Extends the GARCH-LSTM hybrid for volatility forecasting with an ARMA conditional mean and builds forward-bootstrap multi-step prediction intervals, with residual-based innovations and conformal extension to improve coverage.
AI.motivation: GARCH-LSTM hybrids have been evaluated almost only by point accuracy (RMSE, MAPE), and their prediction uncertainty has not been assessed.
AI.method: The authors add an ARMA structure to the conditional mean of the hybrid and develop a forward bootstrap algorithm for multi-step-ahead intervals, using empirical residual innovations for fat tails and conformal prediction principles to lengthen intervals and reduce undercoverage.
AI.result: In simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling forecasts of four US stock indices from 2020 to 2025, the ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid gives intervals closest to the nominal level among the methods compared.
AI.conclusion: Adding an ARMA mean and combining bootstrap innovations with conformal extension gives more reliable volatility prediction intervals for hybrid models.

title: Settling the Burn-in Gap: Sharp Risk Bounds for Tail-Averaged SGD in Linear Regression
summary: We study the excess risk of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression. Building on the instance-dependent spectral framework of Zou et al. (2021), we establish matching initialization-explicit upper and lower bounds on the total excess risk of tail-averaged SGD in terms of the population covariance spectrum $\mathbf{H}$ and initialization $\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^*$ whenever a trajectory spectral feedback condition holds. Existing analyses exhibit a fundamental gap in the effective variance: the upper bound of Zou et al. (2021) retains an undamped contribution from the initial error in the head eigenspace $\mathbf{I}_{0:k^\dagger}$, whereas their lower bound omits the variance induced by the head initialization altogether. We show that both the existing upper and lower bounds are loose: the single-hop fast-mode variance contribution from the head initialization is exponentially damped during the burn-in phase, whereas fourth-moment energy scattered from the head initialization into slow spectral modes during the early burn-in steps survives undamped into the averaging window. We prove that our spectral feedback condition is satisfied in two concrete constant-stepsize regimes: (i) for arbitrary covariance spectra $\mathbf{H}$ and any finite horizon, under an explicit horizon-dependent stepsize chosen prior to execution; and (ii) for polynomially decaying spectra $\lambda_i\asymp i^{-a}$ ($a>1$), under a single horizon-independent positive stepsize. Finally, we complement these positive results with explicit one- and two-dimensional separation constructions proving an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the lower bound of Zou et al. (2021) and showing why fourth-moment assumptions alone cannot determine the asymptotic exponential decay rate without additional structural conditions.

AI.tldr: Derives matching upper and lower bounds on the excess risk of tail-averaged constant-stepsize SGD for high-dimensional linear regression, closing the burn-in gap left by Zou et al. (2021), and gives explicit separation constructions.
AI.motivation: Earlier analyses of tail-averaged SGD have a gap in the effective variance: the upper bound keeps an undamped head-initialization term and the lower bound omits head-initialization variance entirely.
AI.method: Building on the instance-dependent spectral framework of Zou et al. (2021), the authors show that the single-hop fast-mode variance decays during burn-in while fourth-moment energy scattered into slow modes survives, prove a spectral feedback condition holds for arbitrary spectra with a horizon-dependent stepsize and for polynomially decaying spectra with a horizon-independent stepsize, and give one- and two-dimensional constructions.
AI.result: The new bounds are matching and initialization-explicit under the spectral feedback condition; the constructions show an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the Zou et al. lower bound, and fourth-moment assumptions alone cannot fix the asymptotic exponential decay rate.
AI.conclusion: Sharp risk characterization of tail-averaged SGD is possible under a trajectory condition, and extra structural conditions beyond fourth-moment bounds are needed to determine the decay rate.

title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
summary: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Proposes a joint sufficient dimension reduction for regressing a scalar response on a Euclidean predictor and a random object in a general metric space, embedding the object in an RKHS and using a regularized kernel-response envelope with two-stage estimation.
AI.motivation: Regression with both Euclidean predictors and random metric-space objects needs a dimension reduction that differs from the ordinary central subspace of Y given X.
AI.method: A sequential conditional independence framework defines a joint reduction (B^T X, G_Z); the object Z is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a regularized kernel-response envelope extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map, and partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction.
AI.result: The authors establish root-n consistency of the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer and large-sample consistency of the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator; simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the method.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage envelope approach gives a flexible and consistent dimension reduction for mixed Euclidean and metric-space predictors.

title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
summary: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

AI.tldr: Shows that BF16 mixed-precision RL post-training converges more slowly than FP16 because of weight sticking, and that stochastic rounding of FP32 shadow weights to BF16 matches FP16 convergence speed without loss scaling.
AI.motivation: In RL with verifiable rewards, low learning rates make BF16 training converge more slowly than FP16, and the cause was not addressed by the usual remedies.
AI.method: The authors attribute the gap to weight sticking, where round-to-nearest quantization of FP32 shadow weights leaves BF16 weights unchanged for small updates, and replace round-to-nearest with stochastic rounding when quantizing shadow weights to BF16.
AI.result: Stochastic rounding matches FP16 convergence speed across different models and datasets and reduces KL divergence from the reference model relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate, while keeping BF16's dynamic range and needing no loss scaling.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic rounding is a simple fix for the BF16 convergence gap in RL post-training that avoids the KL cost of raising the learning rate.

title: Investigating Composite Modeling in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Design
summary: Scientific design often requires balancing competing objectives that are expensive to evaluate through experiments or simulations. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) addresses this challenge by using probabilistic models to guide the selection of promising designs. In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. We first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations provide no additional predictive information beyond objective values, where composite and black box methods use the same warped Gaussian process prior. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.

AI.tldr: Studies when composite modeling, which learns from intermediate responses that map to objectives through known functions, helps multi-objective Bayesian optimization, finding that gains are larger when the mapping is non-bijective and non-affine.
AI.motivation: Composite modeling improves single-objective Bayesian optimization, but its benefits in multi-objective settings are understudied, and the factors that drive variation in gains are unknown.
AI.method: The authors first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations add no predictive information beyond objective values, then run controlled experiments with four MOBO methods on eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific design benchmarks, comparing against a black-box multi-output Gaussian process.
AI.result: Composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine, supported by the controlled experiments across the benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Composite modeling is most valuable in multi-objective scientific design when the intermediate-to-objective mapping is non-bijective and non-affine.

title: First-order asymptotic expansions for spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians constructed from samples on manifolds
summary: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.

AI.tldr: Derives first-order asymptotic expansions for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric normalized graph Laplacians built from uniform samples on a closed Riemannian manifold with Gaussian kernels, with concentration bounds on the remainders and weak convergence results.
AI.motivation: Spectral convergence results for graph Laplacians on manifolds often assume simple eigenvalues, which excludes general manifolds with nontrivial multiplicities.
AI.method: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed manifold embedded in Euclidean space, the authors expand the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Gaussian-kernel normalized Laplacians to first order and prove concentration inequalities for the remainder terms.
AI.result: The expansions yield weak convergence of the spectral quantities, and the analysis holds without a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians to general manifolds with possibly repeated eigenvalues.

title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
summary: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Uses a tensor-rank framework (CP-MLPs) to show that untied gated MLP blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU are strictly more width-efficient than tied blocks such as ReLU^2 for some target functions, while tied units match symmetric pure-power targets.
AI.motivation: The separate contributions of squared activations, gating and tied versus untied parameter sharing to the expressivity of Transformer feed-forward blocks are poorly understood.
AI.method: Each multiplicative unit is modelled as a rank-1 interaction with a detector role, a value role and an output role. Tied gated blocks force the detector and value roles to share one direction, while untied blocks let them differ, which yields exact degree-wise tensor-rank separations between the two.
AI.result: Untied units are more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, and tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these do not establish a positive approximation gap because approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks keep an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget.
AI.conclusion: The width advantage of untying depends on the target structure, so the choice between tied and untied gating should follow the function class being approximated rather than be assumed universally better.

title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
comment: 20 pages. Code and results: this https URL
summary: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.

AI.tldr: Proposes LENS, a model-agnostic method that selects feature interactions by checking whether a second model trained on disjoint data reproduces each interaction pattern, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features.
AI.motivation: A high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods leave the cutoff to the user, while testing methods need repeated refits or a model of the joint feature distribution.
AI.method: Two models trained with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data are accessed only through predictions. For each feature pair, main effects are removed from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, pairs are ranked by its strength, and a test asks whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction sets the retained pairs, and a strength floor restores selection consistency.
AI.result: On 16 synthetic designs LENS matches leading model-specific rankers such as TreeSHAP and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs. On French motor insurance data it recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained with all pairs. On two credit datasets it selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.
AI.conclusion: Independent replication with a strength floor gives a practical selection procedure that sets its own cutoff and avoids false discoveries; the paper also proves that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits.

title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
summary: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

AI.tldr: Introduces MEOW, a framework that turns non-interactive medical segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners that improve on classes unseen in training without updating learnable parameters.
AI.motivation: Interactive segmentation can use user feedback, but it has remained confined to the open-set setting and does not continually learn from its own predictions over time.
AI.method: MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation, so that knowledge accumulates across interactions and improves future predictions.
AI.result: MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities. The abstract reports no quantitative figures.
AI.conclusion: Open-world interactive segmentation can be achieved without retraining the backbone, which suggests a practical route for medical segmentation models to adapt to new classes and imaging modalities.

title: Forward-Value Discretization: Faster Stochastic Diffusion Sampling Without High-Order Approximation
summary: Stochastic diffusion samplers often require substantially more neural function evaluations (NFEs) than deterministic samplers to achieve comparable sample quality. Although higher-order discretization accelerates deterministic sampling, its benefits for stochastic sampling remains unclear. We establish matching upper and worst-case lower bounds showing that stochastic samplers with higher-order approximations remain first-order convergent, even with exact score functions. Thus, increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce forward-value discretization, a training-free framework that evaluates the data/noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate constructed from previous predictions. For deterministic sampling, the resulting Forward DPMSolver (F-DPMSolver), improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant, despite remaining first-order convergent. For stochastic sampling, we develop Forward DDPM (F-DDPM), which evaluates the model at a cleaner lookahead point adjusted for subsequent noise injection. This estimate reuses both the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise. Both variants admit first-order convergence guarantees with one model evaluation per iteration. Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ, and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines, it achieves competitive sample quality, narrowing the practical efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Shows that higher-order stochastic diffusion samplers remain first-order convergent, and proposes forward-value discretization, which evaluates the model at a lookahead point; the resulting F-DDPM achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets.
AI.motivation: Stochastic diffusion samplers need substantially more neural function evaluations than deterministic samplers for comparable quality, and it is unclear whether higher-order discretization helps stochastic sampling.
AI.method: Matching upper and worst-case lower bounds are established for higher-order stochastic samplers, even with exact score functions. The training-free framework evaluates the data or noise prediction model at a lookahead estimate built from previous predictions. F-DPMSolver is the deterministic variant, and F-DDPM is the stochastic one, which reuses the previous model prediction and the previously injected noise.
AI.result: Across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, FFHQ and LSUN, F-DDPM consistently achieves lower FID than the evaluated stochastic baselines at matched NFE budgets. With 1.5 times as many NFEs as deterministic baselines it reaches competitive sample quality. F-DPMSolver improves sample quality at low NFE budgets through its DDIM-based variant.
AI.conclusion: Increasing the approximation order does not generally improve the convergence order of stochastic samplers, but lookahead evaluation narrows the efficiency gap between stochastic and deterministic sampling, with first-order guarantees and one model evaluation per iteration.

title: Nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Mixtures of Logistic Regressions
summary: Mixtures of logistic regressions provide a flexible framework for modeling binary responses, extending standard logistic regression to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity while retaining an interpretable regression structure. In this paper, we study such models with an unspecified mixing distribution. We analyze a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) and derive nonasymptotic bounds on the estimation error of the resulting mixture regression function under both fixed and random designs. Our results reveal an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius, from which we derive convergence rates under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For computation, we propose a finite-particle algorithm that approximates the sieve NPMLE by optimizing the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution. The method offers numerical advantages over existing algorithms and comes with rigorous convergence guarantees. For any fixed dataset, we establish global convergence of the likelihood to the restricted NPMLE value when the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, we further establish uniform global convergence guarantees and derive error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors. Our analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results in the literature.

AI.tldr: Gives nonasymptotic error bounds for a sieve nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) of mixtures of logistic regressions, and a finite-particle algorithm that approximates it with global convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Mixtures of logistic regressions model unobserved heterogeneity in binary responses while keeping an interpretable regression structure, but the mixing distribution is usually left unspecified and the existing algorithms lack rigorous guarantees.
AI.method: A sieve NPMLE is analysed under fixed and random designs, with an explicit tradeoff between statistical estimation error and the approximation error induced by the sieve radius. The finite-particle algorithm optimizes the locations and weights of a finitely supported mixing distribution.
AI.result: Convergence rates are derived under several tail conditions on the mixing distribution. For any fixed dataset the likelihood converges globally to the restricted NPMLE value once the number of particles exceeds a finite threshold. When the true mixing distribution is finitely supported, uniform global convergence guarantees and error bounds that separate algorithmic and statistical errors are obtained.
AI.conclusion: The analysis also yields a denoising bound for the mixing distribution and an identifiability result that complements existing results, giving theoretical support for both estimation and computation of this model.

title: One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
summary: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUC$_\pi$, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting $\pi$ treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index $J(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) - \mathrm{FPR}(t)$ across cutoffs $t$, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid S]$; for AUC$_\pi$, the decision maker's probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUC$_\pi$ is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by $|\pi(s) - \pi(s')|$ is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUC$_\pi$, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUC$_\pi$ does not.

AI.tldr: Introduces AUC_pi, a decision-weighted AUC, and the policy Youden index, and shows that AUC, the Brier score and AUC_pi are all weighted averages of the same Youden curve J(t) = TPR(t) - FPR(t), differing only in the weights they place on the cutoffs.
AI.motivation: AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score but can rank models differently, and AUC weights every model's cutoffs the same way regardless of how a decision maker acts.
AI.method: AUC_pi weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker who acts with probability pi treats them. Up to normalization it is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. The authors also show that weighting pairs by the absolute difference |pi(s) - pi(s')| is, up to scale, the only fixed pair weight that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution.
AI.result: AUC weights cutoffs by the distribution of all scores, the Brier score by the true probability E[Y given S], and AUC_pi by the decision maker's probability of acting. The policy Youden index, the numerator of AUC_pi, judges every model by the same fixed policy and so avoids the model-dependent cost-threshold weighting that Hand (2009) describes for AUC; the full ratio AUC_pi does not.
AI.conclusion: Ranking measures differ in which cutoffs they emphasize, so the choice should reflect the decision a model supports, and the policy Youden index gives a comparison in which all models face the same policy.

title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
summary: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

AI.tldr: Develops a theory of policy optimization for language model post-training showing that REINFORCE can collapse the probability of optimal responses, and that resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy restores coverage and yields the first global convergence guarantees for PPO- and GRPO-style variants.
AI.motivation: Principled guidance for policy optimization in language model post-training is limited, and it is unclear which algorithms keep the base model's coverage, meaning how readily it generates optimal responses.
AI.method: The authors define coverage-preserving algorithms, whose sample and gradient-step costs are governed by the base model's response coverage. They propose Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized subproblems with reference resets, and apply it to softmax linear policies over pretrained features.
AI.result: REINFORCE can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero even as reward improves, and convergence can then require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage, even with exact gradients and KL regularization. Repeated reference resets mitigate this collapse. Stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, are shown to be coverage-preserving, including those used to train the Kimi models.
AI.conclusion: Regularization, clipping and objective choice determine the sampling and optimization costs of post-training, and reference resets are the mechanism that preserves coverage while allowing convergence to global optimality.

title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
comment: Software paper for a library I've been working on for more than a year
summary: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases as differentiable, learnable primitives.
AI.motivation: Parametric curves are used for continuous feature embeddings, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression, but there is no readable, general library that treats them as learnable primitives with gradients through both inputs and coefficients.
AI.method: The core operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves, and coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules and a functional interface, implemented with classical evaluation algorithms and vectorized PyTorch operations without custom hardware kernels.
AI.result: Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. They show where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. The abstract makes no claim of general speedup.
AI.conclusion: The library offers a readable and maintainable tool for learnable curves, whose computational cost is practical for some problem sizes and substantial for others.

title: Topology-Aware Reinforcement Learning for CAD Decomposition toward All-Hexahedral Meshing
summary: Automatic hexahedral meshing for complex CAD models has long been regarded as the "holy grail" of mesh generation. The fundamental challenge arises from feature misalignment, where orthogonal or interacting features coexist, making direct hexahedral meshing infeasible and requiring decomposition into simpler, meshable blocks. While existing decomposition methods, including frame-field pipelines and learning-based techniques, have reduced manual intervention, they can remain sensitive to geometric and topological complexity and may fail to produce valid decompositions for challenging feature configurations. Specifically, their action spaces are typically restricted to surface-based splitting, which often yields invalid or unmeshable decompositions. To address these limitations, we propose DecompRL, a deep reinforcement learning framework for CAD decomposition toward hexahedral meshing. We design a set of topology-aware internal-splitting actions that leverage both global topological structure and local geometric property to effectively separate misaligned features. Furthermore, we introduce geometric rewards together with meshability feedback to guide the learning process toward valid decompositions and high-quality meshes. Extensive experiments on ABC, Fusion360, NIST, and DeepCAD show that DecompRL achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated learning-based methods on three of the four benchmarks, while maintaining competitive mesh quality. The measured LMFF-to-DecompRL runtime ratio reaches up to two orders of magnitude; this compares the full LMFF procedure with DecompRL decomposition alone, excluding subsequent mesh generation. The largest SR improvement is observed on Fusion360, where DecompRL reaches a success rate of 59.6%.

AI.tldr: Proposes DecompRL, a deep reinforcement learning framework that decomposes CAD models using topology-aware internal splitting actions so that the resulting blocks are valid for hexahedral meshing.
AI.motivation: Feature misalignment in CAD models makes direct hexahedral meshing infeasible, and existing decomposition methods are sensitive to geometric and topological complexity and are typically restricted to surface-based splitting, which often yields invalid or unmeshable decompositions.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning agent chooses among topology-aware internal-splitting actions that use both global topological structure and local geometric properties. Geometric rewards and meshability feedback guide learning toward valid decompositions and high-quality meshes.
