AI.motivation: Overlap-based segmentation objectives favor large regions and systematically suppress sub-3 mm micro-lesions, and pixel-level frameworks lack instance-level modeling, which makes lesion counting unreliable for clinical staging.
AI.method: A centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm uses predicted centroids to condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization jointly; the Volume-Calibrated Loss amplifies the gradient contribution of micro-lesions, and Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization first establishes global representations before progressively unlocking fine-grained localization.
AI.result: MicroBT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on metastases, where micro-lesion (3 mm or smaller) localization precision improves by about 7% and counting estimation errors decrease by about 26%.
AI.conclusion: Centroid-anchored training with size-aware curriculum offers a route to reliable micro-lesion segmentation and counting for clinical staging and therapeutic decisions.

title: CAppleNet: A Coordinate Attention-Based YOLO11 for Real-Time Apple Stem Cavity and Calyx Detection
summary: Automated fruit grading, sorting, and orientation systems require real-time, accurate detection of fruit-level morphological landmarks rather than the fruit boundary alone. This paper presents a custom, fully self-collected and self-annotated dataset of 1506 apple images (1054 training, 301 validation, 151 test) captured under controlled, fixed-camera conditions and annotated for three target classes: fruit body, stem cavity, and calyx. A YOLO11s detector trained with default hyperparameters is adopted as the baseline, and a systematic, one-factor-at-a-time ablation study is conducted across input resolution, data augmentation policy, optimizer configuration, and lightweight architectural enhancement to identify the factors that most improve detection of these fine-grained landmarks under high inter-cultivar color and texture variability. Neither increased input resolution, nor any of six tested augmentation variants, nor manual optimizer tuning improved on the untuned baseline (F1 = 0.9047); only a same-slot architectural substitution of the backbone's C2PSA block with Coordinate Attention (CA) matched the baseline's overall F1 (0.9038) while reducing parameter count by 10.2% and achieving the study's best mAP@0.5 (0.935) and best stem-cavity F1 (0.8217). A confidence-threshold sweep identified 0.15 as the deployment operating point for this model, and a confirmatory experiment combining the CA-swap architecture with the best-performing augmentation variant showed the two effects do not combine additively, reversing the architectural gain rather than compounding it. The resulting design recommendations --- the CA-swap architecture alone, at a 0.15 confidence threshold --- target real-time apple landmark detection for orientation-aware industrial sorting and alignment systems.

AI.tldr: CAppleNet replaces the C2PSA block of YOLO11s with Coordinate Attention for real-time detection of apple body, stem cavity and calyx, matching the baseline F1 with 10.2% fewer parameters and reaching the best mAP@0.5 (0.935).
AI.motivation: Automated fruit grading, sorting and orientation systems need real-time detection of fine-grained morphological landmarks such as stem cavity and calyx, not just the fruit boundary, under high inter-cultivar color and texture variability.
AI.method: A self-collected, self-annotated dataset of 1506 apple images (1054 training, 301 validation, 151 test) with three classes is used; a YOLO11s baseline with default hyperparameters is compared against one-factor-at-a-time ablations of input resolution, six augmentation variants, optimizer configuration and a lightweight architectural change, namely swapping C2PSA for Coordinate Attention in the same slot.
AI.result: No tested resolution, augmentation variant or optimizer tuning beat the untuned baseline (F1 0.9047); the Coordinate Attention swap matched the overall F1 (0.9038) with 10.2% fewer parameters and gave the best mAP@0.5 (0.935) and best stem-cavity F1 (0.8217); a 0.15 confidence threshold is the deployment operating point, and combining the CA swap with the best augmentation reversed rather than compounded the gain.
AI.conclusion: The CA-swap architecture at a 0.15 confidence threshold is the recommended design for real-time apple landmark detection in orientation-aware sorting and alignment systems, since the two effects do not combine additively.

title: The Case for AI-Enabled Gate Monitoring as Farm Security in the UK: A PRISMA-Guided Review of the Evidence on Rural Crime, Livestock Predation and Farm Access
comment: Keywords: farm security; rural crime; livestock predation; camera traps; computer vision; PRISMA; evidence review
summary: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests. We ran a PRISMA guided review: twelve searches of Web of Science and Scopus on 2nd -4th November 2026 returned 1,183 records (761 unique), and grey-literature and hand-searches added 35 assessed sources. We synthesised 96 database records and 24 grey sources narratively. UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records), and the main UK survey of crime and farmer mental health has 80 responses. Cost estimates rest on insurer claims: NFU Mutual put UK rural crime at £41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about £4.5 million and dog attacks on livestock costing £1.95 million. The Home Office states that agricultural crime cannot be separately identified in its central data. We found no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking; light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months in a systematic review of anti-predator interventions; and no study examined how often farm gates are left open or what follows. Camera-trap AI papers report accuracy on ecological datasets, none at a farm gate in the records we found, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts. We argue, as an inference from these gaps and not as a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring, as implemented in Fieldmark AI, would be highly beneficial for UK farm security. It would create the farm-level, time-stamped record that no official source holds, verify events that periodic human checks miss, resolve whether foxes, dogs or people were responsible, and give every other security measure something to be tested against. No study has yet shown that it reduces loss, and we set out the evaluation needed to show it.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA-guided review finds that UK farm security rests on thin evidence and argues, as an inference rather than a demonstrated effect, that continuous gate-level AI-mediated monitoring as implemented in Fieldmark AI would be highly beneficial, noting that no study has yet shown it reduces loss.
AI.motivation: Farm security in the UK rests on thinner evidence than its cost suggests: independent evaluations of rural crime, livestock predation and farm access measures are scarce, and cost estimates rest on insurer claims.
AI.method: A PRISMA-guided review of twelve Web of Science and Scopus searches (1,183 records, 761 unique) plus grey-literature and hand searches adding 35 assessed sources; 96 database records and 24 grey sources are synthesized narratively.
AI.result: UK peer-reviewed evidence is small (16 records); NFU Mutual puts UK rural crime at £41.5 million in 2025, with livestock theft up almost 30% to about £4.5 million; no independent evaluation of cameras, sensors, trackers or marking was found, light and sound deterrents lost effect within one to five months, no study examined how often farm gates are left open, and in one comparison machine learning detected 41% of wildlife against 81% for analysts.
AI.conclusion: Continuous gate-level AI monitoring is argued from these evidence gaps to be valuable, but the paper stresses that no study has shown it reduces loss and sets out the evaluation needed to test this.

title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that rPPG-based deepfake detectors mostly learn video provenance and high-frequency generation artifacts rather than physiological pulse, since their signal appears in background regions, survives normalization and is largely removed by frame shuffling.
AI.motivation: rPPG has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal, but what rPPG-style detectors actually learn had not been established.
AI.method: rPPG-style and CLIP-based detectors are examined on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ using one identically sampled window per video, together with controlled experiments on background versus face regions, frame order, resolution, frame rate, encoding, high-frequency content, injected pulses and self-reenactment, an independent reimplementation, and an audit of official and custom Celeb-DF splits.
AI.result: Simple chrominance traces reach AUC 0.998 on talking-face forgeries, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87); the signal is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band and is equally discriminative from background regions; detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, and a frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds CLIP-rPPG and frequency fusions; official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source content, and custom protocols inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.
AI.conclusion: Reported rPPG gains on deepfake benchmarks largely reflect video source and high-frequency artifacts rather than physiology, and split leakage inflates results, so such detectors need stricter evaluation protocols.

title: Lipschitz-Controlled Flow Matching for Robust Image Restoration
summary: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable. We introduce LipsFlower to reduce this amplification. We derive stability bounds for Flow-from-$Y$, which initializes the ordinary differential equation from a noise-perturbed observation, as well as for observation-conditioned posterior sampling, which conditions the velocity field on the observation throughout integration. Based on this analysis, we develop LipHDiT, a Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer that serves as the vector-field architecture of LipsFlower. LipHDiT incorporates stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation, and convex residual mixing. We also use adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states to penalize excessive sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, the observation. We test both formulations on blind face restoration, measuring adversarial robustness and the perceptual quality of the reconstructions. LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines. These results suggest that Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.

AI.tldr: LipsFlower adds Lipschitz control to flow-matching image restoration through a Lipschitz-aware hourglass diffusion transformer (LipHDiT) and adversarial gain regularization, reducing perturbation amplification while keeping blind face restoration quality competitive with the baselines.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching models can produce high-quality image restorations, but their learned dynamics may amplify small input perturbations and make reconstructions unstable.
AI.method: Stability bounds are derived for Flow-from-Y, which initializes the ODE from a noise-perturbed observation, and for observation-conditioned posterior sampling; LipHDiT uses stabilized approximate spectral normalization, bounded modulation and convex residual mixing; adversarial finite-radius gain regularization at sampled interpolation states penalizes sensitivity to the state and, for conditional sampling, to the observation.
AI.result: On blind face restoration, LipsFlower reduces perturbation amplification while keeping restoration quality competitive with the evaluated baselines, measured by adversarial robustness and perceptual quality of the reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: Lipschitz-aware flow matching can improve the stability of generative image restoration.

title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2025 (Brave New Ideas track)
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP$^3$), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP$^3$ ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP$^3$ ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only $\sim$24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP$^3$ alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: SPY-Bench is a 32,700-sample benchmark testing whether LVLMs can follow user-specified, context-dependent privacy instructions at inference time; most of 21 SOTA models reach only about 24% compliance accuracy, while a Noise Contrastive Alignment variant reaches 96.88%.
AI.motivation: LVLMs are aligned to universal privacy such as credit card data, but privacy is personalized and context-dependent, and no systematic assessment existed of whether models can honour user-specified privacy boundaries at inference time.
AI.method: SPY-Bench contains 32,700 unique image-question pairs with personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, scored with novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness; initial inference-time alignment methods, including a Noise Contrastive Alignment variant, are also implemented.
AI.result: Among 21 SOTA LVLMs, most perform poorly, with only about 24% compliance accuracy even for the top-performing o4-mini, and show limited contextual privacy understanding; the Noise Contrastive Alignment variant achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance.
AI.conclusion: The results mark an initial step toward more controllable LVLMs that can be ethically deployed with user-specified privacy boundaries.

title: A Stage-Wise Explainable Pipeline for Arteriolar-to-Venular Ratio Estimation and Retinopathy Screening
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd IEEE India Council International Conference (INDICON 2026)
summary: The arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) is a clinically motivated marker of retinal vascular health. We present a five-stage pipeline for AVR estimation and exploratory retinopathy screening from fundus images, with inspectable intermediate outputs at each stage. The pipeline combines vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation using a minimal-chord boundary walk, and AVR computation from dominant arterial and venular branches. An explicit threshold-based rule produces the screening decision, enabling errors to be traced to individual processing stages. On an exploratory cohort of 30 HRF images, we report 96.7% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.968 and ROC-AUC of 0.978. Ablation studies and an exploratory comparison with VascX examine the effects of vessel pairing, calibre measurement and aggregation. Interpretation is limited by the small cohort, proxy disease labels and absence of independent reference calibre measurements. The pipeline provides a transparent framework for investigating retinal vascular biomarkers, with further validation needed on larger, clinically graded cohorts.

AI.tldr: A five-stage explainable pipeline estimates the arteriolar-to-venular diameter ratio (AVR) from fundus images and screens for retinopathy with an explicit threshold rule, reporting 96.7% accuracy on an exploratory cohort of 30 HRF images.
AI.motivation: AVR is a clinically motivated marker of retinal vascular health, and the authors want a screening pipeline whose errors can be traced to individual processing stages.
AI.method: Vessel and artery-vein masks, optic-disc localization, vessel-calibre estimation with a minimal-chord boundary walk, and AVR computed from dominant arterial and venular branches, with an explicit threshold-based rule for the screening decision; ablations and an exploratory comparison with VascX examine vessel pairing, calibre measurement and aggregation.
AI.result: On 30 HRF images the pipeline reaches 96.7% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.968 and ROC-AUC of 0.978.
AI.conclusion: The transparent, inspectable pipeline gives a framework for investigating retinal vascular biomarkers, but the small cohort, proxy disease labels and absence of independent reference calibre measurements mean further validation on larger, clinically graded cohorts is needed.

title: Interleaving anatomical inspection and diagnostic reasoning for explainable radiology report generation
summary: Automated radiology report generation can draft clinically plausible reports, yet the pathway from visual evidence to reported findings remains opaque, leaving the diagnostic basis of these reports unexplained and the generated reports difficult to review or revise. We introduce ARIVE (Anatomy-guided Reasoning with Interleaved Visual Evidence), an explainable report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning prior to final report composition. To support this process, we constructed 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) trajectories from MIMIC-CXR, wherein visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation. Trained on these trajectories and further optimized using anatomical and clinical-content rewards, ARIVE achieved superior clinical-efficacy performance compared with strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN. ARIVE's reports were competitive with those of leading models in blinded expert grading, and its MCoT trajectories earned high ratings for diagnostic traceability. Furthermore, a paired review evaluation suggests that access to MCoT can aid in identifying errors within generated reports.

AI.tldr: ARIVE is a radiology report generation framework that interleaves anatomical inspection with diagnostic reasoning before composing the report, trained on 159,416 multimodal chain-of-thought trajectories built from MIMIC-CXR.
AI.motivation: Automatically generated radiology reports can be clinically plausible, but the path from visual evidence to reported findings is opaque, so the diagnostic basis is unexplained and the reports are hard to review or revise.
AI.method: Multimodal chain-of-thought trajectories are built from MIMIC-CXR, in which visual evidence from inspected anatomical regions informs subsequent clinical interpretation; the model is trained on them and further optimized with anatomical and clinical-content rewards.
AI.result: ARIVE achieves superior clinical-efficacy performance over strong baselines on MIMIC-CXR and the abnormality-centered MIMIC-ABN; its reports are competitive with leading models in blinded expert grading, its trajectories earn high ratings for diagnostic traceability, and a paired review suggests access to them helps identify errors in generated reports.
AI.conclusion: Interleaving anatomical inspection with reasoning makes generated reports more explainable and reviewable, and the trajectories can aid error detection.

title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices
summary: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HiPFuse is a point-BEV fusion framework for LiDAR semantic segmentation that reaches 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU on SemanticKITTI and MCD at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on a Jetson AGX Orin, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate.
AI.motivation: Bird's-eye-view aggregation is efficient for real-time robotic LiDAR perception but can mix differently labeled surfaces that fall in the same column.
AI.method: Point and height-partitioned BEV features are exchanged across horizontal scales, with fixed height assignments preserving separate vertical aggregation groups, auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features from the same 3D cells, and a dual-scale BEV context module that adds broader context from a coarser grid.
AI.result: The method achieves 63.7% mIoU on SemanticKITTI at 14.2 FPS and 62.5% on MCD at 22.4 FPS; indoor applicability is shown separately; replacing only the baseline semantic front end in odometry reduces absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and raises accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI.
AI.conclusion: HiPFuse gives accurate, real-time LiDAR semantics on edge hardware that improve odometry and loop-closure recall for robotic perception.
